# emberdays

*Counting the days hot enough to feed a fire.*

<!-- badges: start -->
<!-- badges: end -->

**Documentation website:** <https://etc5523-2026.github.io/etc5523-assignment-4-gauravwarke/>

emberdays helps **people living in bushfire-prone parts of Australia** answer one question:

> *In my city, are very hot days during the bushfire season more common now than in the early 1900s?*

Hot days dry out fuels and drive dangerous fire weather, and rising temperature is the main reason fire weather has worsened in southeastern Australia (van Oldenborgh et al., 2021). The package provides:

- **Data:** `fire_season_temps`, daily maximum temperatures for the fire-season months (September to February) at one Bureau of Meteorology station in each of seven cities, 1910 to February 2019. `stations` describes each station.
- **Functions for the question:** `count_hot_days()` counts days at or above a temperature threshold in every fire season and flags seasons with missing data. `compare_periods()` compares an early period with a recent one. `describe_change()` turns that comparison into one plain-English sentence.
- **Functions for your own data:** `count_exceedances()` works on any daily series with any column names. It counts days above *or* below a threshold in a calendar year, a July–June year or any custom season. `season_year()` labels those seasons. See the [own-data guide](https://etc5523-2026.github.io/etc5523-assignment-4-gauravwarke/articles/your-own-data.html).
- **An app:** `launch_app()` opens a Shiny app where you choose a city, a "very hot day" threshold, part of the season and two periods to compare.

## Installation

Install the package from GitHub:

```r
# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("ETC5523-2026/etc5523-assignment-4-gauravwarke")
```

## Launch the app

```r
library(emberdays)
launch_app()
```

The app uses the data inside the package, so it works offline. The [Get started guide](https://etc5523-2026.github.io/etc5523-assignment-4-gauravwarke/articles/emberdays.html) explains each control and how to read the results.

## Example

How many days of 35°C or more did Perth average per fire season in the early 1900s, compared with the last 30 seasons?

```{r example}
library(emberdays)

perth <- count_hot_days(fire_season_temps, city = "Perth", threshold = 35)
compare_periods(perth, early = c(1910, 1939), recent = c(1989, 2018))
```

Or ask for the answer in words:

```{r example-sentence}
compare_periods(perth) |>
  describe_change(what = "days at or above 35°C", place = "Perth")
```

Results differ between cities, which is why the app lets you choose yours.

## Data source and licence

Temperatures are from the Australian Bureau of Meteorology's Climate Data Online (<http://www.bom.gov.au/climate/data/>), copyright Commonwealth of Australia, as compiled for [TidyTuesday 2020, week 2](https://github.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/tree/main/data/2020/2020-01-07). The script `data-raw/fire_season_temps.R` downloads the raw file and rebuilds both datasets.

Records end in February 2019, so the 2019–20 Black Summer season is not included. Each city is a single station, which may not match conditions on bushland edges.

The package code is released under the MIT licence (see `LICENSE.md`).

## Reference

van Oldenborgh, G. J., et al. (2021). Attribution of the Australian bushfire risk to anthropogenic climate change. *Natural Hazards and Earth System Sciences*, 21(3), 941–960. <https://doi.org/10.5194/nhess-21-941-2021>
